text: Hi guys, for those waiting for the follow-up to the debate with Simple Black Theory, he actually came to my TikTok comment section and admitted that I was right. Not sure if I overlooked it before, but I only noticed it this morning. If this is sincere, then I accept it and I respect that, because it was probably not an easy thing for him to write. And with that, we can finally concentrate on the second part of the argument from the original video. What's the most dangerous, being pregnant, being a cop, or being the pregnant partner of a cop? But what about specifically the pregnant wives of police officers? I normally respond to the video chronologically, but here I want to start with her conclusion. Honestly, where she says, I can't find direct studies done on this topic, is where the fact check should have stopped. Because if you're trying to fact check a very specific claim, that being the pregnant wife or girlfriend of a police officer is more dangerous than being a police officer, and you yourself admit that you could not find direct studies on this topic, then the honest conclusion should be, guys, we don't have direct evidence for this claim. Not, therefore, if you run the stats and compare and contrast, it sounds like it is almost twice as dangerous. No, that is not how this works. That is not fact checking. That is filling the gap with your agenda and calling it fact checking. Now, to be fair, I feel like the point of this comparison is to bring more awareness to officer-involved domestic violence, or DV. So let's see what else was shown in the video. So her argument is that 25-40% of police officer families experience DV, which is higher than the 10-20% of standard reported relationships that experience DV. And to be fair, the 25-40% number is not completely made up. It comes from all the research on officers-involved DV. But this is where we need to be precise. The famous 40% figure comes mainly from early 1990s sources, Johnson's 1991 congressional testimony and Neidick, Russell, and Sang's 1992 preliminary study. In Johnson's testimony, abuse was not operationally defined, so it is unclear how much of it referred to verbal versus physical abuse. In Neidick's 1992 study, physical aggression was measured more clearly, but the study was preliminary and based on a non-nationally representative volunteer sample. And this is not just me nitpicking. A 2016 Mannequin and Rope Systematic Review looked at the available research on this topic, and found that only 7 out of 607 potentially relevant sources actually met the criteria to estimate officer self-reported DV rates. And even among those 7 studies, the estimates ranged from 4.8% to 40%, which already tells you the research is messy. The number depends heavily on how the study defines violence, who they ask, and how the question is asked. So can we say there is research suggesting officer-involved DV is a documented concern? Yes. Can we confidently say that almost half of police families experience DV, as if this is a clean national statistic? No. But even if police family DV is higher than average, that still does not prove that pregnant partners of police officers die at almost twice the rate of police officers. Because DV prevalence and mortality risk are not the same statistic.
